---
title: "Lecture 10: Gaussian Processes and Kernel Methods"
subtitle: "Assumptions, evidence, and uncertainty"
---

## Overview

How much can a few measurements tell us about a function? A Gaussian process uses a kernel to describe how function values vary together, then conditions that distribution on observations. The CO₂ examples show how assumptions affect both predictions and uncertainty, and how uncertainty can guide the next measurement.

- Distributions over functions and Gaussian conditioning
- Kernels for smoothness, trends, and cycles
- Kernel composition and hyperparameter fitting
- Forecast error, interval coverage, and interval width
- GP-guided measurement selection compared with random sampling

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lecture, you will:

- Describe a GP through finite Gaussian vectors and distinguish conditioning from hyperparameter fitting.
- Design kernels for the relationships the problem requires.
- Evaluate uncertainty without assuming that a nominal 95% interval is well calibrated.
- Explain when uncertainty-guided sampling can improve measurement efficiency and what the comparison actually tests.

## Datasets & Acknowledgments

- **Mauna Loa CO₂:** the [Scripps CO₂ Program](https://scrippsco2.ucsd.edu/data/primary-mauna-loa-co2-record/) record. The notebook uses 86 monthly observations from 2010 through February 2017 in the historical `data/archive.csv` included with Lecture 10.
- **CIFAR-10:** an optional notebook extension compares pixel neighborhoods with frozen ResNet-18 feature neighborhoods; no image GP is trained in that comparison. [Dataset source](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~kriz/cifar.html).
- **Libraries:** scikit-learn for GPs and kernels; PyTorch/torchvision for the optional image-feature comparison.
